"Definitely not asking players to support x to get y"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Responding to fears that Marathon's future will dictate Destiny support, Bungie product head Josh Deane encourages players to support only the games they enjoy.

In a lengthy blog post sharing hopes for a "new forever Destiny" and "Destiny 'Legacy'" project, Deane noted that, "we will all tell you that nothing can help bridge us into [the] future more than for Marathon to rapidly evolve and become sustainable."

On the heels of some heady talk of business plans, milestones, and project progress bars, some readers interpreted this as a sign that the health of Destiny 2 hinges on the state of Marathon. While it's surely true that greater success for Marathon would put Bungie in a healthier spot as a business, Deane stresses, in a series of tweets, that "in no way is the Destiny plan contingent upon Marathon."

"I understand my intent is being mistranslated here and that’s on me," he says of his Marathon comments. "Play what inspires you, whatever it is. Mainly hoping we can accomplish our goals in both lanes with a stronger relationship with our entire community!"

"Just looking to serve players that love both/either worlds while we build the future," a separate reply adds. "But definitely not asking players to support x to get y, and not building the plan that way. Just personally believe that there is an empowering force for that future if there is shared encouragement, and respect, as a Bungie community!"

Two additional replies narrow the focus. "Don’t buy Marathon as a donation or offer anything else," Deane says. "It’s our job to show up for you."

"Only buy or play a thing that inspires you from us / you think is cool!" he reiterates. "We will find our way back home with Destiny."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Now-former Marathon game director Joe Ziegler, another in a string of high-profile departures, previously told us that Marathon was never meant to replace Destiny 2, nor did the two games necessarily have a lot of overlap in player appeal. In urgent efforts to bolt on a compelling PvE mode, Bungie's actively injecting a little bit more Destiny into Marathon today.

In September, Bungie acknowledged that Marathon "did not reach as many players as we had hoped." The game's active user base has collapsed since launch – down from a peak of 88,000 on Steam to a daily average in the range of 2,000 or 3,000. Some decline is expected for any live game post-launch, but Marathon is definitely struggling, and it has been for months with seasonal updates failing to rekindle the game.

The player response echoes a feedback loop also seen in Destiny 2 PvP: as lower-skill or casual players leave Marathon, lobbies become more grueling, queue times get longer, and getting into the game or making meaningful progress becomes more difficult with hardcore veterans pouncing on any fresh meat. Marathon's unflinchingly harsh design philosophy already turned some people away at the door, and this spiral only made things worse. But the game's problems, like offering compelling reasons to redo seasonal progression after mandatory wipes, run deeper.

Some people learned to love the pain, of course, as Andy does in our Marathon review. I also put 130 hours into the game in what now feels like a cough syrup fever dream. But after many costly years in development, Bungie's going to need more than a small group of sickos to keep Marathon alive. So even if the two games are decoupled, the future of Destiny and Marathon remains uncertain.

#4111. Arkane survival negotiations reportedly seeing "several forms of takeover" considered ahead of November deadline, as Marvel's Blade production nears end

217 jobs are on the line at the studio, report claims

Update: A Microsoft rep has told PC Gamer that the company have "extended the consultation period by one additional month as we explore options, including finding a partner to support [Arkane] through the development work still ahead." "This is a defined extension," they added, "and we remain committed to keeping the Works Council informed throughout the process."

So, Microsoft's consultation with Arkane's Social and Economic Committee now looks set to roll on until December 13th. Though, as we previously noted, the Printemps Écologique union have said that this consultation deadline isn't the deadline by which Arkane need to have found a buyer, with the setting of the latter deadline being one of the things that needs to take place as part of the ongoing negotiations.

Negotiations over the future of Dishonored and Deathloop developers Arkane Lyon are reportedly seeing "several forms of takeover" considered as a November deadline looms for the divorce Xbox set in motion back in July. French law makes the process of shuttering or chucking away studios a lot harder for companies like Microsoft than it is elsewhere in the world, hence Arkane's fate still being up in the air while production work on Marvel's Blade nears completion according to the report.

French publication Le Monde are behind this paywalled report on how the negotiations between the two sides are going. They note that due to a French law brought in as of 2014, companies with more than 1000 staff have to search for a buyer for three months before they can throw up their hands and shut up shop. In the case of Arkane Lyon, the report says 217 jobs are at risk.

The deadline for these consultations with Arkane's Social and Economic Committee (via Gematsu) is November 13th, though Arkane have longer than that to pin down a buyer for the studio - speaking to RPS, a Printemps Écologique union representative clarified that the exact date is being negotiated and subject to change.

The Le Monde report also cites a representative of Printemps Écologique, who along with the Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Video (STJV) union seemingly aren't too happy with Microsoft's attitude throughout the process so far.

Microsoft have told Le Monde that they're "actively seeking a partner to support the next phase of development and enable the commercialisation of the [Marvel’s Blade] project". According to a union rep cited in the report, the superhero game is "nearing the end" of production, with the unions understandably backing Arkane's work and hoping that it will see the light of day.

Xbox wrote as part of an announcement of layoffs in September - the second of multiple waves in a mass chopping that still isn't over as of writing - that they expected consultation over how Arkane will move forward "to continue through the end of the year".

Solidarity to all of the developers at Arkane and here's hoping these negotiations do end with a result that keeps the maximum amount of them in work and making the games they want to make.

This article has been updated to clarify that the deadline for Arkane finding a buyer isn't the same as the deadline for the consultation period.

#4110. Monopoly Go x The Simpsons crossover is almost here

After a long wait and exhaustive leaks, the highly-anticipated Simpsons event will finally arrive in Monopoly Go very soon, alongside new content.

Monopoly Go players have been looking forward to a major crossover event for what felt like months, and though most of the details ended up leaking, nothing actually beats official information.

The world of The Simpsons has officially arrived in Monopoly Go, and there's a whole lot for players to dive into. The show's creative team even produced a new animated short, featuring Mr. Monopoly, and Mr. Burns.

Available June 3 through July 29, the new event allows Monopoly Go players to jump in the world of The Simpsons. You'll be able to build, and explore all around multiple iconic locations from the show.

Along the way, you'll run into Simpsons characters like Homer, Marge, Bart, Lisa, and of course, Mr. Burns. Developer Scopely teamed up with the show's creative team to create many references, and Easter Eggs for you to discover. You'll find some of those on chance cards, but most of the world has been changed to be part of The Simpsons, including getting to bribe Chief Wiggum to escape jail.

The developer promises a deeply connected world with Simpsons narratives and characters that alter seasonal maps, and offer unique sticker sets and animated sequences to dive in. Incidentally, this is The Simpsons' first appearance in a mobile-exclusive game in 13 years.

Here's a breakdown of everything you can expect, straight from Scopely:

Episodes: Narrative-driven encounters that create stories inspired by The Simpsons. Episodes play out across seasonal boards, sticker sets, and minigames, all capped off with an animated short.

Sticker sets: Every Episode comes with its own limited-time sticker set, taking cues from the latest Simpsons story. Collectible artwork, character journeys and other rewards are yours to claim for the duration of each Episode.

The Simpsons Run: Every two weeks, a new Springfield character will take over the Free Parking tile, kicking off character-driven runs.

Simpsons-themed Shutdowns and Heists: Monopoly Go's shutdowns and heists get a Simpsons makeover, with Springfield-inspired chaos and disasters.

Bribe Wiggum: This changes Go to Jail to allow players to bribe Chief Wiggum, giving you a chance to earn a bigger reward, but not without introducing an element of unpredictability.

Simpsons chance cards: The chance card collection grows with over 50 Simpsons-themed cards full of memes, references and one-liners from the show.

#4109. Rumours Persist That Xbox Spent $500 Million On Gears Of War: E-Day, Despite Some Objections

Update #3 [Mon 2nd Nov 2026, 1pm]: Yet more updates continue to trickle out! To avoid clogging up this original article too much, we've covered the newest information in a separate article elsewhere on Pure Xbox:

News Former Xbox Manager Explains Why $500M Cost For Gears: E-Day Doesn't Tell The Whole Story

Update #2 [Fri 30th Oct 2026, 7:30pm]: In yet another update on this, Bloomberg's Jason Schreier has weighed in on the rumour.

Schreier was discussing BioWare's recent closure when he threw out the Gears of War mention:

"The reality is that BioWare was shut down for the same reason that game companies have been laying off tens of thousands of people over the last few years, which is that game budgets have grown exponentially and become more and more expensive for these companies to make.

We just saw Gears of War: E-Day cost $500 million to Xbox. That is a real number, that is real. That's what we're looking at here - that's what games cost to make, especially in North America these days."

Both Chris Dring of The Game Business and Jez Corden of Windows Central have shared their updated thoughts on this today, with Jez now suggesting that the $500 million figure is correct but he's still not sure how it's distributed.

Original Story: Ever wondered how much money went into Gears of War: E-Day's release this year? Well, we don't have any official figures on this, but a "source" for Kotaku has claimed that Xbox put over $500 million into it.

Their report claims that it's a "source familiar with Xbox’s business", and that the $500 million figure doesn't actually include marketing for the game either. Microsoft apparently didn't respond when asked for comment on this.

Here's a look at the bit from the report in question:

"But according to one source familiar with Xbox’s business, the cost of Gears of War: E-Day is in fact much higher. They told Kotaku it was over $500 million, and that’s before you include marketing."

Kotaku says this makes it significantly higher than the reported budgets of other console exclusives this generation, such as Marvel's Spider-Man 2 which was rumoured to cost around $300 million.

However, not everyone agrees. A few months ago, Insider Gaming journalist Tom Henderson stated on a podcast that he'd heard Gears of War: E-Day cost "upwards of $400 million", which he described as "insane".

Windows Central's Jez Corden then acknowledged this on the Xbox Two podcast, explaining that the $400 million wasn't just for Gears of War: E-Day, as The Coalition works on many other games (Forza, Fable) and even beyond games ("the technological glue for all of Xbox") and some money "is spread across the entire portfolio". He advised that you "can't say" Gears of War: E-Day had a $400 million budget, and that it's "not even the case".

"The $400 million is not all Gears E-Day. You've got to remember that The Coalition is the technological glue for all of Xbox. They don't just work on games, they work on dev tools, they work on Unreal Engine, they work on a lot of stuff beyond simply Gears of War. Some of that money is spread across the entire portfolio. And it's not just the Unreal games either - The Coalition has contributed to Forza, to Fable, to everything. You can't really say 'Gears: E-Day has a $400 million budget'. That's not even the case."

Ultimately, we're not going to get an official answer unless Microsoft / Xbox comes out and says how much the budget was, and that seems unlikely at this point. The figures that are being quoted are certainly extravagant, but we're inclined to believe what Jez is saying about the budget being spread across far more than just one single game.

In any case, we absolutely love Gears of War: E-Day, awarding it a rare 10/10 score at launch!

Review Gears Of War: E-Day (Campaign) - A Monumental Triumph For Xbox, And My Game Of The Year

E-Day exceeded expectations and made me fall in love with the series even more

Feature Gears Of War: E-Day (Multiplayer) - Playing Horde Siege And Versus Makes Me Feel Like A Kid Again

It's the most fun I've had with the series since Gears of War 2

I also disagree that no one cared before. Were you not alive during the 8-bit and 16-bit console wars, they were in many ways far more polarising than the current 3 horse race, people absolutely did care how Sega v Nintendo were doing. Though I agree it was less about financial targets and more “mine is better than yours, if sold more, or scored higher, or has better graphics”.

Yet the reality is we live in a different time, back then a studio could output a game every year, or several a year with much fewer staff and a relatively small budget. A game could fail, or several games could fail in a row, and your studio would often keep going regardless. That isn’t the case now. There are REAL stakes involved now, and failure could mean the end of a company you love (RIP BioWare et al) or an IP you want to see more of. There’s a totally valid reason it is different now.

I also agree SOME people will just use it to console war - that is both sad and undeniable true - but many of us want to know because it directly affects us when these companies or games do poorly and we no longer get to see games and IP love, and see the brilliant creators of our hobby out of work. I'll copy my comments from other articles here:

E-Day is definitely in trouble if you just look at Steam. Its peak high for the past 24 hours is just 7,565, which for a game of its scale, that cost so much, and which only came out a couple of weeks ago is truly terrible. Oh, and just by way of comparison, Helldivers 2 had a peak high of 46,648 over the same period, and that game came to Steam February 2024, added to which, that 24 hour peak high is 15,000 higher than E-Day managed at its peak! So yes, E-Day is in significant trouble, and I say that as someone that absolutely loved the Campaign, and also bought the Collector's Edition.

Obviously Game Pass could well be a factor on both PC and Xbox, but I imagine that even with that, the drop off will be similar to that seen on Steam where it started with a peak high of about 31,500. In other words, Steam has seen something like 75% fewer people playing the game now than occurred when the game first released just two weeks ago, and I imagine that it will be much the same among those of us that bought the game on Xbox, and also Game Pass on PC and Xbox.

Losing 75% of your gamers in the space of 2 weeks is not good.

As for The Coalition, bearing in mind that Sharma still needs to find over 1000 job cuts, I think they will suffer badly, and go someway to addressing her redundancy problem.

I expect The Coalition to be cut to the bare minimum, with just enough people to do a year of seasons for the game (which will then just be repeated every 3 months just as happened with Gears 5, which is still having seasons to this day). Once work on any DLC and the seasonal work is complete, I expect them to switch to finishing the PlayStation version, where it will likely release either the end of next year, or the beginning of 2027. Basically, I think The Coalition will become a zombie studio, mortally wounded, and probably done for within 2 years. E-Day could easily be the last game we get. I know that sounds totally apocalyptic, but you cannot make a game costing upwards of half a billion, and sell so few copies, and have a 75% drop off of players within the first 2 weeks. Whether the existing community will hang around and keep playing, and crucially, keep spending in the game, I'm not sure. When you see such a significant drop in player numbers so quickly after release, it does not usually bode well for a game (or a studio)...

Microsoft's biggest problem, as I've seen it over the decades, is that they often seem to lose patience.

They invests heavily, expects the market to respond, and when dominance doesn't materialise quickly enough, they change direction, restructure or abandons the project altogether.

That's particularly damaging in gaming, where customer loyalty and confidence take years to build

Mobile: Windows Phone couldn't overcome Apple's and Google's established ecosystems

Music: Zune was a decent product, but Apple owned the market with the iPod/iTunes

Web browsers: Internet Explorer dominated, then Microsoft lost ground to Chrome and Firefox

Search engines: Bing has struggled to dislodge Google, despite Microsoft's enormous resources.

Gaming: Xbox entered as a serious competitor, but Sony and Nintendo continued to maintain stronger identities and customer loyalty.

Microsoft has the resources and cash to compete with almost anyone. What it seems to struggle with is accepting that having deep pockets doesn't mean it gets to dictate the market.

As I've said before, Xbox as an ecosystem can survive, but hardware? I'm not particularly hopeful for the future of Helix.

#4108. Woim is the earth-guzzling, self-bisecting sokoban pick-me-up I needed after a week of games industry disasters

While ladling city-builders into the Maw's feeding trough this week, I remarked that being a worm must really suck. Then came the closure of BioWare, layoffs across other EA studios, further depressing genAI revelations, allegations of antisemitism at indie gaming events, a big Capcom data breach, and yet more worrying tidyings about Arkane.

I rescind my earlier observation: I would like to be a worm. A happy little worm, tunnelling after golden apples in the moist and forgiving earth, where there are no emails or press releases at all. The only thing I have to worry about down here is my butt growing so big I get stuck behind it. And also getting chopped in half by sliding doors, but it turns out this may actually help with the first problem. See for yourself - video below.

Ah, to be a soil-dwelling invertebrate in Woim, a puzzle game with a touch of the sokobans, consisting of 50 levels and an unspecified quantity of secrets, scattered across four subterranean worlds. The idea in each level is to crawl around a grid layout to reach a golden apple, opening the exit.

As with non-videogame worms, this involves a certain amount of ingesting earth and pooping it out behind you, but you can't just devour the whole layout. You'll need to guzzle red apples that make you longer, so that you can (for example) keep pressing a switch with your body as you slither towards a door. Or you might have to shove a rock onto that switch. Or shove that rock onto a water jet to propel it somewhere you can't reach.

Later on, there are breakable eggs that must be carried to nests, daisies that push back outward when you take your weight off them, scissors with which to snip yourself into separately functioning halves, and hats. I don't think this is an entirely accurate worm simulator. As in sokoban, the major problem is trapping yourself, but you can undo moves without penalty by tapping Z.

I've played six levels, and it's a jolly production. The music wobbles and boobles along, and your worm has a habit of looking at you expectantly when you get stuck that makes me giggle. Read more about it on Steam. If, unlike me, you've had a really uplifting week and are in sore need of a sokobanlike charged with maximum ontological dread, may I recommend Void Stranger.

#4107. Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Switch 2 Development Team Has Been Revealed

Nintendo has just released the first two parts of a new Ask the Developer series all about The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time on Switch 2. Alongside a bunch of interesting insights about the game's development, the interview also finally reveals the development team behind it.

As it turns out, the Switch 2 remake was developed internally by Nintendo's Entertainment Planning & Development (EPD) Production Group No. 3 — the team that has handled just about every Zelda entry since the early 2000s.

The remake saw HokWai Ng take on the role of Director (his first Dir. role at the company, though he also worked on Tears of the Kingdom), with Aya Shida (Pikmin 3, Mario Kart 8 Deluxe, Tears of the Kingdom) on Art Direction, Hiroki Taguchi (Breath of the Wild) as the Program Director, and Masato Ohashi (Animal Crossing: New Horizons, Splatoon 3 Expansion Pass) as Music Lead and one of the Sound Directors.

There was a part of us that thought Nintendo might bring in another studio to work on the remake — particularly as it increasingly appeared more and more faithful to the original — but it's nice to see that it was an inside job instead. Worry not, Zelda legends Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi both served as producers on the project.

Parts three and four of the OoT Ask the Developer series will be released tomorrow (3rd November), so we're sure that there are even more dev stories to come. Gosh, what a week to be a Zelda fan!

#4106. "This was not a Creative Assembly developed game": Total War boss points the finger at external partner for Shogun 2 Complete Edition disaster

But concedes that "we took our eyes off" its creation

Last week, Creative Assembly and Sega pulled Total War: Shogun 2's remastered Complete Edition from Steam, after an avalanche of complaints about technical problems and some AI-generated art. Now, Total War vice president Roger Collum has written a personal apology, while pinning some of the blame on an unnamed external partner. He's also clarified Creative Assembly's stance on generative AI, conceding that the studio do use it to help with "analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping", but that they're against using it to generate game assets and art.

"I get many of you are angry and disappointed about the state of the Shogun 2: Complete Edition release," Collum writes on the official Twar Reddit. "We are too – especially the team members who have put everything into Total War games for years, some even decades. This was not a Creative Assembly developed game. It wasn’t subject to our same internal reviews and quality assurance. We took our eyes off its external development, with all our teams focused on our next big projects. However, whatever the development arrangements, Total War is our franchise and our name is on it."

Again, Collum doesn't name the external developer in question, but Mataboo Games are listed as co-devs on the Steam page. Collum says that SEGA and a small team of senior developers are working with the external team on "next steps", with details to follow. In the meantime, he has some general thoughts on how and when the Twarfolk make use of generative AI tools.

"I want to be very clear on the studio-wide stance on generative AI, because I know there are many questions about where we stand," Collum writes. "We are a craft studio. Our games are made by incredibly talented people, and we do not believe in a world where technology replaces the creativity of humans. At Creative Assembly we do not use generative AI to create game assets, including AI-generated art. We demand the same of any external developers we work with. The situation with Shogun 2: Complete Edition is being investigated."

Collum adds that Creative Assembly do, however, use AI tools for "support" purposes. "It shouldn’t replace the creator," he says. "I don’t believe that AI can replace the human experience, judgement and creativity that awesome experiences come from. Can AI tools help with analysis, debugging, or speedy prototyping so our experts can focus on making incredible games? Absolutely."

Collum ends his message by requesting that people don't abuse individual Total War developers. "Our community teams, QA, designers, and everyone in between are doing their job, as asked by the company," Collum writes. "Their safety is our priority. They do not deserve, and we will not tolerate, harassment or being singled out online and personally criticised." Collum warns that if you're nasty to developers, the studio may need to be less transparent in future.

I'm not sure I wholly buy the argument about "taking our eyes off" the game, given that Creative Assembly and Sega ran a bunch of trailers and marketing for it and sent round a FAQ detailing, among other things, how it would affect mods. While unavailable for purchase, the Complete Edition's Steam page is still live as of writing with "overwhelmingly negative" reviews. Creative Assembly and Sega have reinstated the original game's Steam page while they work on kicking the CE into shape.

#4105. New Mass Effect Cancelled So EA Can Focus on Star Wars Battlefront 3

The next Mass Effect game was cancelled and BioWare shut down because publisher EA wished to focus on a new Star Wars: Battlefront title instead of bringing both to market.

That is according to a new Bloomberg report from journalist Jason Schreier, who explains the situation EA was facing a few months ago.

As the publisher was reviewing its upcoming portfolio, executives "found themselves with two sci-fi action games that were each projected to cost hundreds of millions of dollars: Star Wars Battlefront III and the next Mass Effect title". As a result, they decided to go with the Star Wars game because it was seen as a "less risky, more predictable bet".

Schreier says Star Wars Battlefront 3 hasn't even entered development yet at EA DICE and Respawn Entertainment, yet the publisher still opted to go with it over Mass Effect.

There were other factors at play in relation to the closure, like the reception of BioWare's more recent games (Mass Effect Andromeda and ANTHEM), and the disappointing sales of Dragon Age: The Veilguard. The latter resulted in EA heavily cutting the RPG developer's workforce, and when it was closed last week, just 50 employees remained at the studio.

News EA Scrubbing Mass Effect from Other Games as Series Starts to Die Off

Future cosmetics for Battlefield 6 event removed

News Save Mass Effect Petition Rockets Past 200,000 Signatures as Fans Ask EA to Continue the Series

However, the driving force behind BioWare's closure was the investment needed to bring Mass Effect to market, and the risk it represented when compared to Star Wars Battlefront 3. Schrerier concluded the piece with: "Game budgets have grown exponentially while sales have not, driving game companies to shift development outside of North America and focus only on their biggest franchises moving forward."

Since the news broke last week, fans of the Mass Effect series have rallied to try and save it by starting petitions and paying for billboards to advertise the campaign. Seemingly, though, it's all going to be in vain.

#4104. BioWare staff "should be given the first opportunity and the federal support" to buy the studio and keep it running, says Canadian political party leader

Hope. It's in short supply at the moment. Regardless, I hope that something a Canadian politician's proposed in a post scoring easy likeability points at the expense of EA's recently installed owners comes to pass, no matter how unlikely it is to do so at this point. Rather than being unceremoniuously shuttered, leaving the world staring down the barrel of a future without new games from a storied studio, BioWare should be handed over to its staff with backing from the Canadian government.

Nationalise BioWare, basically. Well, sort of. "The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio," is what Avi Lewis, leader of Canada's New Democratic Party, wrote in a post following the closure. "They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity - and the federal support - to buy it and run it themselves. And if we want to avoid the Mass Effect effect in Canada, we should be keeping private equity out, not welcoming it in."

You can almost hear the horde of suit-wearing money-knowers who've sensed that suggestion's been made and are about to descend from orbit to yell about taxpayers' money being used to help ensure the creation of future adventures starring space blokes who say 'We'll bang, ok?'. I should also point out that since I'm not Canadian, it wouldn't be the country I live in spending some of their cash on helping the Veilguard avoid being veilgone to the depths of the vault where EA keep Burnout and ten million other defunct series people would like to see return.

The developers at BioWare know how to run the studio. They know how to make the games we all love. They should be given the first opportunity - and the federal support - to buy it and run it themselves.

In all seriousness, I'm not totally sure it'd work out in the long run, but it's something. An alternative to a company erasing a studio from existence because the Saudi Public Investment Fund and Jared Kushner have been allowed to load them up with a ton of debt rather than reaching further into their own pockets.

So, I say screw it. Set up a new position called Minister for BioWare to ensure the devs have what they need to get their heads down that next Mass Effect which reportedly had a trailer leak the other day. Just make sure it's not some right-wing crank, or BioWare might run into some of the same problems it'd been feared their generally very inclusive games might face under Saudi ownership.

#4103. Talking Point: What Are You Playing This Weekend? (October 31 - November 1)

It's officially the spookiest day of the year, but do you know what you're playing this Halloween weekend?

October has been a pretty wicked month for gaming. And so, as we play out its final hours, we'd like to know what it is you're having a crack at. This is the space to have a chat with your fellow PXers and let us know what you're up to. If you're still looking for something to play, make sure to check out our Shocktober Sales roundup, alongside this week's Free Play Days games too.

Alrighty then, let's get into it. Here's what we're playing on Xbox this weekend:

Happy Halloween, everyone! Or, as I'm a Manxie, I should be saying Hop tu Naa! 🎃

My plans for this weekend have changed a smidge. Originally, my goal was to crack on with the phenomenal Silver Pines, as well as aim for its Mythic cheevo. Toss in a bit of Gears of War: E-Day's Halloween event and fully revel in the spooks.

Instead, I am now getting properly stuck into Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 in order to bring you a lovely little review of the sucker. The whole N/A for Xbox on Metacritic got me all bothered, and so I've decided to get Pure Xbox in the review mixer.

I'd expect it won't take me all weekend to get through the Campaign, play some DMZ and vibe with Multiplayer, though. So, who knows? Maybe I will get to play something spooky for Hop tu Naa!

I've been really, really tempted to pick up the new Evercade Nexus alongside the Banjo-Kazooie and Banjo-Tooie Double Pack, but I've held off for now. Maybe I'll just play on my Evercade Alpha this weekend instead.

On Xbox, I've still got tons of Star Wars: Galactic Racer I want to play, while the new release of Tape to Tape is definitely on the list as well. I've been waiting so long for that game to arrive on Xbox, and now it's finally here!

I’m playing the appropriately spooky Seance of Blake Manor on Game Pass.

It’s set in 1897. You play a detective summoned from Dublin to investigate a disappearance at a remote hotel in the west of Ireland, where a group of guests have arrived to participate in a seance. You’ve got to speak to them and also snoop around to find clues as to what’s happening. All the guests and staff also have their own backstories as to why they are there.

It’s great fun once you get to grips with it. The best detective game I’ve played since the Golden Idols and probably better than them.

Taking a little bit of a break from Fortune’s Weave this weekend in an effort to make some progress on the rest of my games before GTA, so I’ll be playing Well Dweller, Control Resonant, Belmont’s Curse, and Galactic Racer.

I expect I’ll probably be able to finish Well Dweller, which feels like a breath of fresh air in being so short after Fortune’s Weave literally already being my second most played game ever in the Switch ecosystem of consoles (and with a legitimate chance to leap past Tears of the Kingdom very soon).

For some reason, Belmont’s Curse hasn’t clicked for me, which is sort of bumming me out as a massive Castlevania fan. I don’t know if it’s the artstyle or the fact that Well Dweller just feels so much better immediately, but the game feels just sort of ok so far and I hope that changes.

Galactic Racer is fantastic and I love it. It’s far better than I expected, but I should’ve known this one is literally for me, being a big fan of the previous podracer games.

And, man, I cannot believe we’re in a universe where I didn’t drop everything to play a Remedy game, but here we are. I’m wondering if I’ll get anywhere in Control before GTA. #4102. Nintendo Wanted To Remake Ocarina Of Time To "Trigger New Insights" For Future Titles

"Hang on, why is Nintendo remaking Ocarina of Time again?" It's a natural question that might have occurred to you in the last few months, and in the latest Ask the Developer interview, Series Producer Eiji Aonuma had the answer.

Part of the reason for returning to the title, it turns out, was to try to "trigger new insights" from the developers that may feed into future Zelda games. "Many of the team members who work alongside me on Legend of Zelda games today have only experienced developing the more recent titles," Aonuma-san says. "That led me to wonder, 'Do they truly understand just how significant The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was to the series as a whole?'"

"I started to wonder how they'd interpret The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time as they go about developing future Legend of Zelda games," he continues. "By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development."

While he describes the potential behind such insights as "extremely valuable," he also notes that it wasn't the only reason he wanted to return to OoT for the series' 40th anniversary. The game's structure is drastically different from more recent series entries like Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, two games that a whole generation of Zelda fans will have grown up on (as sobering a thought as that is), so Nintendo wanted to showcase a different style of gameplay, too:

In The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, part of the fun comes from progressing through a carefully paced adventure and story, gradually building up the player’s growth and their understanding of the narrative along the way. We wanted players who had grown accustomed to Legend of Zelda games like Breath of the Wild, where they can freely choose their own path from the start, to experience that kind of gameplay as well

Whether revisiting Ocarina of Time actually does influence any future games' design decisions remains to be seen, but if you're looking for GoodGameTM inspiration, it certainly isn't a bad place to start.

The Ask the Developer interview also revealed that Ocarina of Time was internally developed at Nintendo, with HokWai Ng in the Director's seat.

How do you hope Ocarina of Time informs future games' designs? Let us know in the comments.

The Blood of Dawnwalker, the debut title from Rebel Wolves, is one of the year's best releases, and my personal pick for GOTY 2026. While it's likely to be passed up by more critically acclaimed horror games like Resident Evil Requiem and, for the top award this year, GTA 6, I found it to be a delightfully old-school horror RPG with gothic vibes galore and a story worthy of multiple playthroughs. The secret sauce, according to the studio itself, is not to chase any current trends, but to make the game that you yourself want to play.

Korean publication Inven (via Otakukart) recently visited the Rebel Wolves headquarters in Warsaw, where studio leaders shared insights into their game development philosophy. Not unreasonably, the developers just want to make games they want to make without influence from the stock market or industry trends. Speaking on the studio's founding, a Rebel Wolves spokesperson described by Inven as "a marketing representative" said: "We wanted to create an environment where we could focus entirely on the project itself without being driven by stock market pressure or tight deadlines."

While Rebel Wolves does receive support from outside backers like minority stakeholder NetEase and The Blood of Dawnwalker publisher Bandai Namco, it's still an independent studio with full creative control over its games. With The Witcher 3 director Konrad Tomaszkiewicz as co-founder and CEO and other ex-CDPR devs working at the studio, there are obvious Witcher influences in The Blood of Dawnwalker, but the game very much has its own identity that I'm looking forward to seeing expanded in the sequel. That's because, in the studio's words, "We are rebels. We don’t want to follow trends. We want to make games that we ourselves want to play and enjoy."

What exactly that looks like probably won't come into view for quite some time, but it's very possible it'll include The Blood of Dawnwalker's somewhat controversial time limit mechanic. I thought the timed quests were a genius way to add stakes and consequence to the game's missions, but understand the potential for FOMO some other players have experienced.

6 things I need from The Blood of Dawnwalker's sequel

#4100. Future? No Thanks! dev removes AI-generated voices from game and offers refunds to players who feel "betrayed"

Next game will be"completely hand-coded".

Open world ecosatire Future? No Thanks! has been updated to remove some AI-generated voices, after lead developer Paolo "Molleindustria" Pedercini belatedly disclosed his usage of the technology earlier this week. He's also offering to refund people over Paypal or Venmo if they "still feel betrayed" by this.

The update removes two instances of text-to-speech generated voicework for in-game robot characters – an automated toilet and an automated translator in a hair salon. In his previous blog, Pedercini wrote that he used genAI for these characters as a spoof of generative AI. He's decided to replace them with human voice-acting following a number of angry reactions on social media and some coverage in the press.

"The voices were recorded earlier this year but I decided to not use them because I thought the actual uncanny text-to-speech was funnier in that context," Pedercini writes in a new blog post. "Alas, the new generation of text-to-speech counts as user-facing AI-generated content and that keeps creating all sorts of annoyances and bad optics."

Pedercini still thinks the text-to-speech voices belong in Future? No Thanks! "In my opinion the game is worse now, but only, like, 0.001% worse," he observes. In less acrimonious tidings, he's also tweaked the game so that the "various gigs give you a bit more money, possibly preventing some situations of soft-locking players from achieving all the quests."

The blog includes a "personal update" in which Pedercini expounds rather bitterly upon the backlash to the game's genAI elements. "Somebody from Bluesky (the Twitter/X clone) dragged me due to a post disclosing what I foolishly thought a minor use of generative-AI in Future? No Thanks!" he writes. "I gave versions of that statement multiple times before, whenever asked by festivals and events. Steam doesn’t require disclosure of generative AI for things like code assistance so many people assume their favorite indie games don’t use AI at all just because the developers stay mum."

For context, Valve updated Steam's rules in January to allow "efficiency" tools, such as coding assistants. I'm basing this on anecdotes and conversations with other devs, rather than any kind of statistical survey, but it seems very likely that a lot of developers on Steam aren't disclosing their genAI use - the policy has always been more of a gesture on Valve's part than a mechanism of real accountability.

"Not me, I’m a good boy and I wanted a page I could link to that explains that NO, this is not a vibecoded slop game but YES, I did ask chatGPT to fix a broken shader and a few things like that," Pedercini goes on. "More foolishly, I added a paragraph that sounded like I was trying to exculpate myself by poo-pooing on all the colleagues that advocate for an AI-free life." (The paragraph in collection was deleted after the original blog's publication, but not before it had been screengrabbed and shared on the socials.)

"Look, it was not a good post," Pedercini concedes. "Defeatist, hastily written. I thought nobody would read it. Anyway, slow news day, everybody fucking hates AI, the whole scene piled on."

Pedercini proceeds to caricature some of the people yelling at him over social media: "Am I satirizing the puppy killing machine by KILLING PUPPIES?" He compares the anger he's received to being harrassed by Adam Baldwin's followers at the height of the Gamergate hate campaign.

Pedercini ends by sharing a list of developers who've sworn off generative AI. "Big props to them," he writes. "Give them a follow. SteamFest is drowning in actual slop, help them stand out. And I hate to break it to you, but you should probably assume that all the studios that have not made a public statement against all generative AI are using it for coding in some capacity. I’m guessing this episode isn’t going to encourage more voluntary disclosures." As for his next game, it'll be "completely hand-coded".

#4098. Factorio's final major update has rolled off the assembly line, adding "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for"

Including QoL tweaks, new visuals, and more predictable asteroids

In one of the happier endings to occur in games this week, impossibly enormous resource management sim Factorio has just released its last-ever major update – version 2.1 – on its stable branch. As previously heads-upped by developers Wube Software, 2.1 doesn’t make any big new additions to its planets or tech trees, but does sneak in more than 30 quality of life improvements and minor new features for both the base game and its Space Age expansion. Including, they say, "the things we wanted to do for 2.0 but didn't have time for." Nice to get a few final pieces out the door before it closes, eh.

There’s also an updated trailer, if you want to watch promotional footage for a game that may well have enveloped your every waking moment since 2016.

Factorio - Trailer 2026 Watch on YouTube

Here are some of those changes I’ve picked out at random. "Mixed rockets: Rockets can now carry multiple different items in one launch, so no more sending a full stack of everything just to build a small platform." Nice! "Land mines can be used as tripwires and enemy detectors." Devious! "Asteroid damage now depends on the asteroid's remaining health instead of its speed, so it is much more predictable." Convenient! Not counting how you’re still being hit by an asteroid. There’s also now the ability to play Space Age without the controversial Quality mechanic, as well as the ability to flip pumpjacks and burner miners instead of merely rotating them, like some loser.

The 2.1 update also gives Factorio one last graphical polish, including a handful of new models and a "new pump rendering system that can connect to fluid wagons no matter how cursed your station is." I’m merely pretending to be a Factorio expert for the purposes of publishing this article, though I will say – from experience building piplines in Deep Rock Galactic – that a series of tubes is only truly cursed if it still works, in spite of itself, at transporting liquids. Otherwise you’ve just got a pile of broken pipes, again, like some loser.

This isn’t the end-end of Factorio, which Wube Software have said will continue to get bug fixes and support-level updates while they largely move on to "other game prototypes/experiments." Though even if it was, it’s had a bloomin' admirable run, starting with four years of early access - successful enough to cement it as the de facto basis for later automation-builders like Satisfactory and Dyson Sphere Program – and continuing to enrapture aspiring industrial managers into the present. Ollie has over 1,000 hours in it. Maybe I’m the loser for making light of it.

#4097. New Call of Duty to Remove 'Appalling' Footage of Real-Life Tragedy

Families criticised Activision for including videos

Activision has apologised and promised to remove footage of a real-life tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

Victims’ families understandably reacted angrily when it emerged that news footage from 2022’s Itaewon disaster was included in the game to illustrate a fictional invasion from North Korea.

The videos show people being removed in stretchers, in body bags, and more.

The Itaewon disaster occurred during a Halloween event four years ago, when more than 100,000 people assembled in a narrow alleyway, causing some to get crushed. Almost 160 people died, and many more were injured.

Bereaved families described the inclusion of the footage as “highly inappropriate and senseless”, prompting publisher Activision to respond. It’s said the videos will be removed in the game’s next update on 12th November.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the publisher said it had “not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape, or form”. It offered its condolences to the victims’ families, and apologised for including the video.

Review Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 (PS5) - Same Old Multiplayer Drags Down Stellar Package

As the Editor of Push Square, Sammy has over 15 years of experience analysing the world of PlayStation, from PS3 through PS5 and everything in between. He’s an expert on PS Studios and industry matters, as well as sports games and simulators. He also enjoys RPGs when he has the time to dedicate to them, and is a bit of a gacha whale.

#4095. Mass Effect 3 ending discourse ignored the RPG's scale, ambition, and exuberance, including that of its oddly great co-op

Ah, come on, it was fine. Better than fine. We can argue for another fourteen years about whether BioWare should have redone the ending or not, but Mass Effect 3 was really a compendium of endings, a ludicrously ambitious wrapping-up of dozens of plot threads, character arcs, and running gags. Even if you can point to other RPGs that, on an individual basis, are more branching and reactive, Mass Effect 3's largely successful closing of a galaxy's worth of choose-your-own adventure books - filled in and followed across three evolving instalments - showed an audacity and grandiosity that no other three-part series had matched before. Or, at least on that scale, has pulled off since.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

It didn't hurt that Mass Effect 3 also had the trilogy's fiercest, bangiest action by far, nor some of its highest-stakes, often most lip-chewing moments of decisionmaking. It is true that the accumulation of War Assets wasn't always as heavy on character drama as the game-long preparation for Mass Effect 2's Suicide Mission, but then you don't simply play Mass Effect 3 to make a number go higher. You play it to punch or hug reporters, to love or shoot your friends, to save or damn entire species. And it has loads of that, right up to the point to have to choose the colour of an explosion. Potentially beyond, if you treat the (assuredly, delightfully) fanservice-forward Citadel expansion as Shepard's true last ride.

Back in 2013, and again with 2021's Legendary Edition, I was sad that Mass Effect 3 ended and glad that it happened. That, at the risk of appearing less furious at EA's stewardship than I am, does not change with BioWare's closure. What does bother me is the uncertainty over what now happens to Mass Effect 3's surprisingly entertaining, weirdly long-lived co-op mode.

I don't doubt this was put in for boring, C-suite, "gamers want multiplayer" reasons. But that only gave the resultant palled-up superpower maelstroms a sense that they were better than they had any right to be, with explosive moments of player-to-player power synergies and spacious, blindspot-filled maps that could maintain a thrilling feeling of being permanently surrounded. Post-release additions to the species-spanning character roster also showed glimpses of that same, fuck-it swagger that BioWare exhibited in the campaign, as they increasingly moved away from familiar soldier archtypes towards electric whip wielders, regenerating lizards, teleporting ninjas, and three-foot-tall psychic asthmatics. While many of today's co-op shooters fret over miniscule balance changes, in pursuit of some mythically perfect meta, Mass Effect 3's gave you a crate of action figures and told you to go nuts.

While I haven't played it recently, there's a small but loyal contingent who do, and for their sake I hope the multiplayer's P2P setup helps it survive the EA cull. I was, and for now technically still is, too good to be doomed to oblivion. Or, worse, vibe-coded Legendary Edition mods.

#4094. I've got egg on my face because Steam's Personal Calendar feature has apparently been a test this whole time and is only now actually a fully fledged component

I'll be honest folks: I didn't know that Steam's Personal Calendar feature was still technically in testing. I've been using it here and there to keep track of what's come out recently or what's coming out imminently, and have generally found it to be fairly reflective of the kinds of games I was interested in. It just worked! Yet lo and behold, a post from Valve went out yesterday announcing that the feature has launched out of Steam Labs "and is considered a full feature of the Steam Store."

The feature, if you've missed it, is "another way to see recommended games for you, showing both recently released and upcoming games filtered down to the set of games we think you are most likely to be interested in," as Valve explain it anyway. "It uses your recently played games to find people with similar playtime profiles to you, and then looks at the games those players have been adding to their wishlist or playing." I do wonder if there's a bit more going under the hood here, as my playtime count is all over the place, with nothing above 50 hours on there, and that's an exception to the norm (I'm from more of a console background, alright).

But even still, my recommendations do remain pretty good, showing me games that I have since added to my wishlist. I'm never opposed to new discovery tools, especially considering how bad Valve can actually be at that kind of thing. Apparently the recommendation system refreshes daily "to incorporate the latest data. In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day, but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the 8-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

This comes as part of a broader swathe of changes Valve have been introducing to Steam over the past couple of years, including one from last month that will change its homepage discounts and events section to be a bit more algorithm based. Perhaps it's some kind of weird prepwork for that new Half-Life they're almost definitely making but only talk about accidentally.

"RuneScape is going to be here for another 25 years"

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Several species of fly have lived longer than RuneScape Reignited, a relaunch of one of the oldest MMOs around. It would've seen fresh servers filled with new accounts soft-reset the game while veterans continue playing as they were.

Developer Jagex apologized for and quickly canceled this plan within weeks of its grand RuneFest-side reveal after those veteran players complained that they felt left behind or sidelined in favor of efforts to entice new players.

Many RuneScape fans are relieved to see Jagex act on feedback and preserve the current game, some people are disappointed to miss out on a new account race or just a fresh start, and others seem unclear what the heck Jagex was even trying to do. I spoke to RuneScape creative director Ryan Philpott, known to players as Mod Ryan, to unpack things.

Reignited was set up as a capstone for the Road to Restoration update plan that has seen Jagex, in the past year especially, cut out much of the systemic and monetization rot that reduced RuneScape to a much less popular MMO than its sibling Old School RuneScape. Indeed, part of this plan is to put RuneScape "in a place where it can stand alongside Old School Runescape, as an example," Philpott says.

"We felt that there was a great opportunity," he says of the Reignited planning. "So much is going on inside the game, the game is in the best place it's ever been – or has been for at least 5-10 years – and as part of that, we thought about what a great opportunity there is to open those doors again and allow players to come in."

I used the term relaunch in the interview, and Philpott says he's done the same internally. But "it wasn't just, 'Let's find new players,'" he says. "That wasn't the only goal. The goal was: this is such a great game, how can we break through the wider bubble and put this game on the map?"

The makers of RuneScape want a second chance, in many ways – an opportunity to show players what they believe to be a much healthier and more fun game than RuneScape's reputation would imply. Philpott says what they didn't want is a split in the game, or two parallel versions of RuneScape.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

"You mentioned that fork in the game," Philpott responds. "We didn't really consider it that because, ultimately, it's similar to releasing other game modes. Iron Man came out, Group Iron Man, etc. There are other ways to play the game." Reignited was meant to be the same, and Reignited worlds may have been merged with the main worlds eventually, Philpott suggests, but some players read it as a whole new branch that would dilute the game's population and paper over past achievements.

"I think there was a little bit of miscommunication," he adds. "No one was losing anything," but it didn't always feel that way. Some messages got mixed between RuneFest talks, player interpretation, and follow-up blogs from Jagex. The idea was "to share in that moment where it feels like a fresh launch," but players worried that the game they've known, which was only just getting back on its feet, would be upstaged by a new version that never faced the same systemic issues. And in an MMO with this much horizontal account progression, starting fresh means losing a lot.

Philpott says Jagex expected "some pushback," if only because you can't please everyone, but there was "more conversation than I would have anticipated" after the Reignited reveal. He touts the rapid response to that discourse, and Jagex's decision to cancel Reignited, as a sign that the company is better about gauging player opinions before acting, and shows it won't sacrifice the current experience in an effort to grow the player base.

"We're not against changing our minds," he says. "We want to do what's best for the game. It's been here for 25 years because of our players and making these decisions. To make it here for another 25 years is always about making the right calls." With Reignited dead, the next big push will be December 2, which Philpott says is still the second-best time to start RuneScape. The best time, he reckons, is now.

A lot of this comes back to that second chance. Next year, Jagex will focus more on rebalancing and pushing more agile updates – answering the "374 days since we asked for this" Reddit posts.

Philpott maintains that RuneScape is a much better, healthier game than it was even a year or two ago. Working on it now is a "night and day difference in a positive way" compared to those darker times, he says, and though he "would have loved" to remove the likes of Treasure Hunter sooner, it feels "great" to have the game free of so much gunk.

"We will not make those mistakes again," Philpott says. "RuneScape is going to be here for another 25 years and I'm super excited. One, about the end of this year. Two, about next year, And three, about where we're going to go in the next three, five, seven, nine years."

#4091. Paralives' first major update slips to next year, but when it comes you can expect some pretty meaty improvements for all of its main features

Since launch back in May of this year, life sim Paralives appears to have been trucking along nicely, with the dev team offering up fairly regular updates with all sorts of tweaks big and small. Certainly confidence-inspiring for an early access game, especially one as systems-driven as it is. And now, the Paralives team have outlined their plans for the game's first major update, which seem very catered to improving the core experience.

As part of a four point plan they outlined, first up on the docket is "buffing up the basics." This is all about strengthening some of the currently existing Live Mode systems. That means improvements to how relationships function by unlocking more things when a relationship level goes up, adding in more interactions that change your Para's emotions, improving the Community Centre's bundles and tweaking the economy curve so it isn't as easy to get money.

The next point is on expanding the Live Mode, meaning the addition of a pair of new skills, adding in more together and story cards, new relationship label unlockables, and more jobs too. Build Mode will also see some improvements, with a big focus on build breaking bugs. You can also expect new bits of furniture and items, and a tweak to furniture and item efficiency.

Lastly, there are also planned improvements to the Paramaker. One is by adding in more hairstyles and clothing items, notably baggy outfits, and the other is increasing the range of fat and muscle sliders "to represent a wider variety of body shapes." As a bigger person myself I'm always enthused when character creators actually let you have a fat body, so this is a welcome point from the dev team.

Worth noting that this list "is not final," and some things may be pushed back with others getting added in. Also worth noting is that while this first major update was planned for the end of 2026, it's been pushed into next year as the team needs a bit more time. You can read about all of these plans in more detail over on Steam.

#4089. Xbox follows in PlayStation's footsteps, introducing AMD FSR 4.1, targeting better graphics and performance on Series X/S

AMD, the company that designs the chips inside Xbox and PlayStation consoles, made a big announcement this week: it's bringing the latest version of its advanced, AI-driven image upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to Xbox Series X, Series S, and handhelds ROG Ally and Ally X.

An older version of FSR is already supported on Xbox, but FSR 4.1 is its most advanced release. You may recall FSR 4.1 arrived on Steam Machine and Steam Deck shortly after the former's launch in the summer, and it has proven to be a useful option for players looking for a sharper image.

FSR works by rendering the game at a lower resolution, which is then upscaled to a higher resolution by using machine learning algorithms. This allows supported hardware to deliver better quality visuals without putting extra strain on hardware, or by giving more consistent performance.

While all Xbox platforms stand to benefit from FSR 4.1's arrival, Series S and the more hardware-constrained Ally and Ally X handhelds could see the biggest gains. In that way, Microsoft is extending the life of the Series consoles by allowing its aging hardware to do more.

The timing of this announcement is particularly notable, too, as just a couple of weeks ago, Sony introduced QSSR - a similar machine learning-based upscaling technology - for PlayStation 5. QSSR is the less capable sibling of PSSR, which is exclusive to PS5 Pro.

FSR 4.1's arrival also comes as new reports suggest Xbox's next generation Project Helix consoles could cost upwards of $1,800, which would significantly hinder its adoption rate, considering its price.

"We've worked very closely with AMD to optimise this technology, giving developers another powerful tool for great performance and visual quality for players," said Xbox chief technology officer (CTO) Scott Van Vliet.

"And this is just the beginning. Our teams are continuing to work together across hardware and software, and there's even more ahead with Project Helix, leveraging FSR Diamond to power what comes next."

AMD did not offer a specific date as to when FSR 4.1 will arrive on Xbox Series consoles, but it's going to be interesting to see how the image quality compares to PS5's QSSR.

#4088. HELENA : Cloud District is a megastructure photography game laser targeted at my interests, and it's out next week

Yes, I'm doing it, I'm writing about a megastructure game for the second time this week because come on, HELENA : Cloud District just looks stunning, don't it? Admittedly there's a chance you've not heard of it, that be the way of things in this algorithmically dominated world, but allow me to tell you about its big, scary world and the strange camera you're equipped with to capture all the sights it holds.

In the world of HELENA : Cloud District, you have come across a rotting megastructure that appears to be long abandoned, all sorts of strange flora dotted throughout it. In one part, it's something of a precision first-person platformer, as you navigate its intricately layered world with drops so steep you'd probably die before you hit the bottom. At the centre of it all is a computer, and it's here where you must bring all of your photographs in order to learn more about the history of the place.

The in-game camera itself is a fascinating thing to look at, completely impossible, alien and ancient in its design. From what I can tell it's a sort of metallic helmet, these insect-like segments snapping into place when you're gearing up to take a snap. You only appear to have three photo slots at any given point in time, meaning you can't just go gallivanting around the place all trigger happy like. There's an amount of care you have to put in positioning yourself and subsequently finding your way back to the central computer.

It's non-linear too, there's no set path you have to take, and it seems like there's some neat movement mechanics too. "Slide, hover, and glide through the structure in your own creative way in order to reach every level and get deeper into the slumbering Cloud District," explains the game's Steam page. Sounds like you don't have to worry too much about that falling to your death thing, then. I'm quite enthused by what HELENA : Cloud District is putting down, and it has a release date now too: October 29th. Same day as Hypnos! I now dub October 29th megastructure day. There will not be a vote on this matter. Ahead of HELENA's release, make sure to give it a wishlist on Steam.

#4087. World of Warcraft: Forever's beta has been extended, as community members mourn the loss of their hunter pets

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta has been extended until this Friday, much to the joy of the community of early players.

Announced on X by World of Warcraft's Associate production director Clayton Stone, this extension will allow those who have hopped into the MMO for their level 1-30 journey to spend just a little bit more time before servers go down this weekend.

In addition Blizzard is hosting a server stress test today, allowing players - including those who otherwise wouldn't have access to the beta - a chance to hop on and bush the game to its limits. After the servers go down on Friday, WoW Forever lovers will have a chance to reserve a character name next week, ahead of the full launch on the 4th November.

This obviously is great news for those who can't get enough of World of Warcraft: Forever, but there's a funny consequence to this extension. On World of Warcraft community hubs, players made lovely farewell posts to the game ahead of the original beta end date. Like this one, where Reddit user Roodster123 sat their gnome down overlooking the Stormwind docks in a post titled "This is where I leave you little one. We had a good run. Until we meet again."

Another user No_Staff_6299 made a similar post titled "Wait for me Kitten, I'll be back soon." In it, we can see their character crying and dismissing their pet spider, never to be seen again. A hunter's pet is rather important in World of Warcraft, so if they want to play the beta some more, they'll need to capture a new one - no doubt it'll be a pet with far fewer fond memories attached. The comments on that post are full with other hunters sharing their similar stories. "Lets pour one out for u/No_Staff_6299" wrote user Thirteenera, in reaction to the news.

While it's maybe a little late to hop on now, World of Warcraft: Forever's beta gave an excellent first impression to the upcoming MMO. That obviously is brilliant for those excited to dive back into Azeroth, and equally tragic for those of us unable to get time off work.

#4086. Why is PC gaming outpacing consoles? "PC players have a bit more choice," analyst says

"Slower growth for console compared to PC and mobile," analyst predicts

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's never been easier to recommend PC gaming, so it sucks that it's rarely been harder to build a gaming PC. With consoles struggling and their market long since mature, PC gaming is responsible for a lot of the annual growth in the industry. It regularly surfaces a much more diverse lineup of top games, and more developers (especially in Asia) are investing more in the platform. But what gives PC gaming an edge?

I spoke to Emmanuel Rosier, Newzoo's director of market intelligence, about the growth of PC gaming. Some of the benefits are obvious. For example, PC gamers have Steam, a central storefront with strong features, they have more input options between M&K and controller support, there's better mod support, graphics have a higher ceiling, and a PC is useful for more than games and streaming. But there are a lot of other contributing factors.

"I had a look at that, because it's quite interesting when you look at the business models," Rosier says of PC and console differences. "When you look at the business model on PC, half of the revenue is coming from microtransactions because a lot of PC games are free-to-play. A lot of PC games are everlasting live services, and on console premium is still the biggest share, the biggest business model."

Even on console, however, the biggest premium games are iterative sports franchises or similar behemoths like Call of Duty, so they're still comparable to live services as "more of a continuation" of an experience. "You can consider it recurring revenue coming from within the same franchise," Rosier says.

This is less pronounced on PC. Sports games are much smaller on PC, for one, but it also "probably has to do with the audience somehow," Rosier adds. When you look at reports like Newzoo's and examine the most profitable or most played games each month, PC consistently surfaces more newcomers and indies, even if the top 10 are still stuffed with heavyweights like Minecraft, Fortnite, and Roblox.

Big Walk is a useful example: it got more user traction on PS5 because it was included in PlayStation Plus, but that meant it made way more money on PC. (It skipped Xbox over the BDS boycott, just as indie darling Celeste has now done.)

"PC players have more choice in general," Rosier says. "For a lot of indie publishers, it's easier to first release your game on Steam, on PC, and then if it works expand to console. PC players have a bit more choice, which means there is a bit less concentration of the bigger title, just because there is so much more choice around it."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Newzoo forecasts growth for the overall games market, but "slower growth for console compared to PC and mobile." Consoles are struggling to find success in Asia (particularly outside of Japan, Nintendo and Sony's home turf), but PC gaming is booming in huge countries like China. Consoles are also really struggling with pricing, and a new generation risks pricing out even the people who've been rebuying consoles generation over generation, to say nothing of new players who already aren't replacing aging gamers on core platforms.

PC is also dealing with its own AI data center-fueled price hikes, but Newzoo finds that "PC keeps growing" regardless. This is about more than new users, for one, and Rosier suggests there's still probably a lower barrier to entry to PC gaming right now just because "you're more likely to have a computer at home. Looking at those AI costs, Rosier reasons that "the initial effect of AI on video games is a bit negative for the consumer because they are stuck," land-locked in the consumer market from Hell.

"PC is really surfing on a very positive wave for the past two or three years," Rosier finds. "It's quite interesting, because if you look back at 2015 to 2020, PC was almost flat and consoles were booming with all the live service, Fortnite, everything. But now it's kind of the opposite.

"It's kind of like there is a ceiling for console but PC keeps growing. I was discussing with my team earlier this morning, and they say we're probably going to need to revise up the PC forecast for 2026 because the first-half result for some publishers on PC is really good, higher double-digit in some case There is this really strong momentum for PC, and I think the fact that PlayStation decided to release some of their games on PC, and they moved back, but I think it pushed a bit more players to go play on PC because they had access to almost every exclusive."

Once you're able to try PC gaming, it can be hard to go back. The platform's certainly not without its issues – horrible ports, Windows missteps, and fiddly settings, for three – but I'm definitely not the only one spending more and more of my game time at my desk, even if I still love my couch and my three consoles.

Can anyone overthrow Steam on PC? "As long as Valve is independent and not a publicly traded company," analyst says it looks impossible

Austin has been a game journalist for 12 years, having freelanced for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, IGN, Sports Illustrated, and more while finishing his journalism degree. He's been with GamesRadar+ since 2019. They've yet to realize his position is a cover for his career-spanning Destiny column, and he's kept the ruse going with a lot of news and the occasional feature, all while playing as many roguelikes as possible.

#4085. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs": Gloomwood's publisher isn't too keen on using the term immersive sim despite it being one

You know, I think at this point in my life there is a non-zero chance I will die before anyone is able to settle comfortably on what defines an immersive sim. I'm not going to even try to! The idea is too annoying and I'm sure someone will disagree with some aspect of it. And if you ask New Blood boss Dave Oshry, when it comes to trying to flog an immersive sim, it's probably best to not even refer to it as one.

"Is it a good marketing term? No. It sucks," Oshry told PC Gamer in a recent interview. "It's awful." For those unfamiliar with New Blood, they're a publisher of some pretty cultishly popular games like ULTRAKILL, as well as immersive sims like Gloomwood and Fallen Aces. Ironically, though, it's through publishing Gloomwood and working with lead dev Dillon Rogers specifically that he even heard of the term. "He's like, 'That's what these are called'. I'm like, 'I have never heard that before in my life. What the fuck are you talking about?'"

That doesn't mean Oshry had never heard of or played an imsim before, he was familiar with classics like Deus Ex, he just considered them to be a different genre: RPGs. "System Shock and Deus Ex, they were RPGs. People called them RPGs. That's the funny thing about an immersive sim. You're immersed in this world. You're building your character. Yeah, that's called an RPG, brother. That's a roleplaying game." Perhaps a controversial statement amongst the diehard imsim fans, but perhaps not an entirely untrue statement either.

In Oshry's opinion, "if you market something as an RPG, I think you'll do better than marketing it as an immersive sim." This part I'm not sure I'd entirely agree with. Sure, everyone knows what an RPG is, but they do also have certain expectations that come with them, such as stats and the like that you don't typically find in imsims. Ahah! Maybe that's the difference. Immersive sims are RPGs without the stats. By golly, I've done it without even trying. Either way, this Oshry fellow does seem to be pretty good at peddling weird little indies, so maybe I should just pipe down.

My original plan was to give it an hour or two tonight after some traveling, that hour or two turned into five and I'm still playing. It's more of an experience than a game, one people really need to see for themselves. I went in completely blind and was blown away by the visuals and the aesthetic. I don't recall having ever seen stop-motion animation in a game before, it feels like a Tim Burton film in the best ways possible. I lost myself and my real surroundings so quickly, and I wasn't alone either I had Potboy by my side. I really can't get over how well sculpted the characters and the world are.

The music too is fantastic. I think I'll need to look into the soundtrack when I finish. The jazz is so spontaneous in it's arrival and departure as it makes way for sweeping Scandinavian folk music. It reminds me of the first time I watched Taxi Driver and heard Bernard Herrmann's score and the saxophone solos by both Ronnie Lang and Tom Scott. The whole game feels so haunting, isolated and yet so hopeful. It's scarier than Until Dawn too, I've been running and hiding from all kinds of creepy somethings, it's perfect for Spooky season.

I'm also going to work on upgrading my dwarves and gear in Deep Rock Galactic Survivors. It's harder than most games in the genre, and there's not a lot of room for strategy when you are being swarmed by hundreds of giant bugs, I still haven't beaten a Tier Three run. I do like that it has a gear system though, it has the usual permanent stat upgrades that you'd expect too. Having items you can equip adds a lot more to the gameplay loop. The mining is a nice twist too. I'll probably work on some Ballxpit too, that's been my main portable game while I was away. Overall I'm just happy that I finally played some Horror games, and might play even more.

My mind thinks it's three in the morning though so I'm going to pause my Midnight Walk and do some sleep walking instead. This spooky weekend I am finally playing The Blood of Dawnwalker on PS5. What. A. Game. I have been pleasantly surprised by what this game offers, and its unique experience with time management.

I like how personal the entire narrative feels. It manages to accomplish what other open world games fail to do: provide a sense of urgency. More often than not, there are games set in a sprawling world that threatens the end of existence but allows you to explore and take your time, undercutting the story. Dawnwalker doesn’t skimp on this at all.

It’s been a long while since I’ve played an RPG that had me genuinely questioning my actions. With its unique time mechanic, I’m thinking of what quests — main and side — I should prioritize. You would think this would be a hindrance, and restrictive, but it actually enhances the experience because it respects your time.

The writing is top-notch because each quest feels important, thus the feeling of missing content due to time doesn’t seem like a loss. You never feel like you’re making the wrong choice in what to focus on.

Moreover, I find all of the characters to be really intriguing. I’m invested in their stories and curious to see how my decisions impact them. There have been a few reactions that have caught me off guard. Even minor, typical open world tropes such as “clear out this encampment” make a meaningful difference. Once again, the world feels alive and significant because I’m making decisions that can alter the outcome in drastic ways, to people whom are struggling to make a living, but also living in constant fear.

The combat is also really fun to me. It’s not for everyone, but once you get a grasp at the parrying and the many abilities at your disposal, it becomes an intense battle of nutrition. That’s not to say it’s not without its jank. You can get stuck on corners. And once you are in a confined area you are committed. The lock on can also be finicky at times, but it also adds to the adrenaline.

Overall, I’m really impressed by this game. It obviously has The Witcher DNA in terms of graphics, combat, and world design, but that’s not a bad thing, is it? And what better way to end this review by quoting the classic saying, “It’s always darkest before the dawn”.
